article.title: States Legalize Online Casinos
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. State budgets are tight again. Legislators want new money that does not arrive as a new income tax. Online casino games, usually called iGaming, keep surfacing as an answer. A bill appears, an industry coalition promises a revenue windfall, and advocates start asking who will actually be paying. The product under debate already sits on every phone, licensed or not. One example, meant only for adults where online gambling is lawful, is a Thai-language roundup of บาคาร่า websites, cited as an illustration and not an endorsement. Legal status depends on the map. A few countries grant private licenses, others keep online casinos inside a government monopoly, and many prohibit them. In the United States each state decides for itself, so the reader's own state law is the one that counts. What Exactly Are States Being Asked to Legalize? iGaming means real-money casino games played online. That covers slots, blackjack, roulette, baccarat and poker, run by licensed operators under a state regulator. It is a separate question from sports betting. Sports wagering spread quickly after the Supreme Court struck down the federal ban in 2018. Online casino games have moved far more slowly, and only a small group of states allow them. Pennsylvania shows the scale once a state says yes. In August 2026, the monthly revenue report from Pennsylvania's gaming regulator put online slots revenue at $195.2 million. Online table games added another $48.1 million. All gaming in the state produced $249 million in tax revenue that single month. Numbers like those are why the bills keep coming back. What Do Supporters of Legal Online Casinos Argue? Supporters rarely claim gambling is good for people. Their case is that it already happens, so the state should regulate it. Their main points run like this: ● Revenue. Taxes on operator winnings can fund schools, transit or health programs without touching income tax rates. ● Consumer protection. Offshore sites often skip age checks and offer no dispute process. A license can require identity checks, deposit limits and self-exclusion tools. ● Problem-gambling funding. A statute can earmark a fixed share of tax for treatment, prevention and research. ● Visibility. Regulated operators must report data, so lawmakers can see who plays and how much they lose. Some of these points have real weight. A player on an unlicensed site has almost no recourse when something goes wrong. Why Do Critics Call It a Regressive Tax? The strongest objection is about who carries the cost. The Rockefeller Institute's study of state gambling revenue over time found that gambling money comes largely from low and moderate income households. It also found a recurring pattern of quick gains followed by slower growth or decline. That decline has known causes. States compete with neighbors for the same players. New products also cannibalize older ones, so an online casino can pull money from a lottery or a retail floor. The same study flags a further equity issue: expansion can cut into tribal casino income, and many tribal nations rely on it. Robert Reich made a version of this argument years ago. He described legal gambling as a regressive tax on people with the least to spare. A phone app sharpens the concern, because a casino floor closes and an app never does. Whose Losses Fund the Tax? This is the part campaign materials tend to skip. Every dollar of iGaming tax is a slice of player losses. Operators earn their margin from a built-in house edge, and the state then taxes that margin. So a revenue projection is also a projection of losses. A forecast of $300 million in yearly tax implies a much larger sum lost by residents. Lawmakers can reasonably ask which neighborhoods those losses will come from. Promotional credits complicate the math further. Some states let operators deduct free-play offers before tax. That shrinks the public share while marketing keeps growing. What Would a Fairer Bill Include? Neither side has to win outright. A bill can be written to take the critics seriously. Common proposals include: 1. Problem-gambling funding fixed in statute, not left to yearly appropriation. 2. Default deposit and time limits that players must actively change. 3. Limits on advertising, especially during televised games watched by teenagers. 4. Independent research on losses by income and zip code, published every year. 5. Formal consultation with tribal nations whose compacts could be affected. 6. A sunset clause that forces a fresh vote after review. Photo by Mariya Eskina on Pexels Voters there rejected both sports betting measures in 2022, partly over who would profit. Earlier coverage asked how big a California sports betting market could be , and the money question quickly crowded out everything else. Frequently Asked Questions About Online Casino Bills Is Online Casino Gambling Legal In Every State? No. Each state decides, and most have not authorized online casino games. Sports betting is far more widely legal than iGaming. Does Online Casino Revenue Close a State Budget Gap? Seldom by itself. Gambling revenue is a small share of most budgets, and growth tends to slow after the first few years. Who Pays for Problem-Gambling Treatment? That depends on the statute. Some states earmark a set share of tax, while others leave it to annual budget fights. Why Do Tribal Nations Follow These Bills Closely? Many tribal compacts were negotiated around exclusive rights to casino games. A statewide online market can affect both that exclusivity and tribal revenue. Weighing the Promise Against the Price The iGaming debate is less about morality than about distribution. A state can raise real money, and it can also add consumer protections that offshore sites lack. The open question is whether the people losing that money are the people the state most needs to protect. Any online casino play is for adults only, and only where it is lawful. This article is not legal advice, and it does not offer financial guidance either. Gambling is entertainment, not a source of income, and the house always keeps an edge. Anyone struggling can call the free, confidential national helpline at 1-800-GAMBLER, available around the clock.
